chunks: From him, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Ma'alla Abu Uthman, from Ma'alla ibn Khunays, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

I asked him about a man who travels and rides in the sea. He said: 'It is disliked to ride in the sea for trade, for indeed your father used to say: 'Indeed you harm your prayer.' That is it; the people find their livelihoods and sustenance.'

key_terms.تُضِرُّ بِصَلَاتِكَ: You harm your prayer / Neglect your prayer
key_terms.رُكُوبُ الْبَحْرِ: Riding in the sea / Sea travel
key_terms.يُكْرَهُ: Disliked (makruh) - a juristic category of ruling

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on sea travel for trade in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In this narration from Imam al-Sadiq (AS), the dislike (makruh) of sea travel for trade is rooted in the practical difficulty of maintaining regular prayer (salat) amidst the uncertainties of maritime journeys, contrasting with the general populace who accept this trade-off for sustenance. This reflects the Shia juristic emphasis on preserving the quality of worship even when engaging in permissible economic activities, a principle often discussed in the context of 'tahdhib al-ahkam' regarding the balance between livelihood and spiritual obligations. The mention of the Imam's father, Imam al-Baqir (AS), underscores the continuity of this specific juristic insight within the Ahl al-Bayt's scholarly tradition.
